Heb.7.8.sup: Supplied in English. The Greek leaves the subject of this half unstated.

_extra.1: δὲ (and, but): added by the Greek translators; nothing in the Hebrew answers to it.

03.n: The Greek has no 'your' here: just 'you reap a harvest'.

07.n: The Greek adds 'your': 'in your field' again, where the Hebrew says 'in the field'.

09.n: Swete's text reads ἀναστραφήσῃ, from ἀναστρέφω, to turn back. Rahlfs's edition reads a longer compound here, ἐπαναστραφήσῃ, so the matched dictionary form (ἐπαναστρέφω) belongs to that reading, not to Swete's.

11.n: The Greek word is προσήλυτος, 'one who has come over'. English 'proselyte' comes from it, though here it still means a resident foreigner, not a religious convert.

17.n: The Greek translators wrote κύριος, 'Lord', for the divine name. It is the same word the servant uses for his master in Matthew 25:24 on this page.

Mat.25.24#01.r: The third servant comes up to his master to give his account.

Mat.25.24#02.r: Moves the story on to the last servant.
Mat.25.24#02.n: The BSB's "Finally" is an interpretation of this small connective. The Greek only marks the next step in the story.

Mat.25.24#03.r: He too comes, like the two servants before him.

Mat.25.24#04.r: The article turns the following phrase into a description of a person: the one who had received.

Mat.25.24#05.r: Points back to the single talent already mentioned in the parable.

Mat.25.24#06.r: One talent, against the five and two given to the others.

Mat.25.24#07.r: A unit of weight, used as a sum of money.
Mat.25.24#07.n: Abbott-Smith gives the order of meanings: first a balance, then what is weighed on it, then a sum of money equal to that weight. The amount varied by place and period. The English sense of talent as a gift or ability grew out of this parable.

Mat.25.24#08.r: He had received the talent and still had it.
Mat.25.24#08.n: This is a perfect participle: the receiving is finished and its result still holds. That fits a servant who kept the money unused.

Mat.25.24#10.r: A slave addressing the man who owns him.
Mat.25.24#10.n: The same word stands for God's name throughout the Greek Old Testament. STEPBible tags this occurrence with its human sense, master, which accounts for 82 of its 691 verses. The translations split between Lord, Master and Sir.

Mat.25.24#11.r: He claims a settled judgment about his master's character.

Mat.25.24#12.r: The master himself is the object of what the servant claims to know.

Mat.25.24#14.r: The servant's charge against the master: demanding and without mercy.
Mat.25.24#14.n: Abbott-Smith derives the word from a verb meaning to dry, so its root picture is stiff, dry and rough to the touch. It describes rough, hard things as well as hard men. Abbott-Smith files this verse under 'of men: hard, stern, severe'.

Mat.25.24#15.r: States the master's character as fixed, not occasional.

Mat.25.24#16.r: A generic word for a human being, here used of the master.

Mat.25.24#17.r: Present participle: a man who habitually reaps.
Mat.25.24#17.n: Abbott-Smith notes that the Septuagint chiefly uses this verb for Hebrew קָצַר, the reaping verb that opens Deuteronomy 24:19 on this page. In that verse itself, though, Swete's Septuagint uses a different reaping verb, ἀμάω.

Mat.25.24#18.r: Introduces the fields he reaps without having sown.

Mat.25.24#20.r: The master takes a crop he did not plant.

Mat.25.24#21.r: Joins the second half of the charge.

Mat.25.24#22.n: Abbott-Smith's entry for the verb that ends the verse, scatter, names this one as its opposite. Here the two describe the threshing floor: gathering what someone else winnowed.

Mat.25.24#23.r: Points to the place the grain came from.
Mat.25.24#23.n: Abbott-Smith treats it here as shorthand for 'from the place where'.

Mat.25.24#25.r: Throwing grain into the wind to separate it from the chaff.
Mat.25.24#25.n: Abbott-Smith classes this verse under 'of winnowing grain', and lists another use: of property, to squander. The KJV's 'strawed' is an old form of strewed. The BSB reads the word as sowing, 'scattered seed', which is a different farm picture from winnowing.

Deu.24.19#01.r: Sets the scene: whenever harvest comes.
Deu.24.19#01.n: Most of the older translations read 'when'. The BSB's 'If' makes it a case law. The Hebrew particle can carry either sense.

Deu.24.19#02.r: You cut your grain at harvest.
Deu.24.19#02.n: Gesenius gives the first sense as TO CUT OFF, especially grain, and so to reap. The KJV and Geneva keep that picture with 'cuttest down'.

Deu.24.19#03.r: Your crop, the thing being reaped.
Deu.24.19#03.n: The noun comes from the same root as the verb before it, so the Hebrew reads 'reap your reaping'. The Douay-Rheims says 'the corn', which in older English meant grain. The BSB folds the noun into its verb and does not render it separately.

Deu.24.19#04.n: Gesenius gives the primary sense as a plain or level tract of country.

Deu.24.19#05.r: A sheaf left behind by oversight, not on purpose.
Deu.24.19#05.n: Gesenius cites this very verse for a special sense: to leave something behind through forgetfulness. The Douay-Rheims spells out both halves: 'hast forgot and left'.

Deu.24.19#06.r: One bound bundle of stalks, left lying in the field.
Deu.24.19#06.n: BDB separates two words spelled this way: this one, a sheaf, and another, the omer, a dry measure. No Gesenius entry was matched to this word in our parsed copy.

Deu.24.19#07.r: Still lying where it was cut.

Deu.24.19#09.r: Do not go back over the field for it.
Deu.24.19#09.n: This is the ordinary Hebrew verb for turning and returning. Gesenius notes that it is also used figuratively, of a sinner turning back, but here it is literal.

Deu.24.19#10.n: This is a very common verb, with a meaning as wide as English 'take'. Geneva's 'fet' is an old form of fetch.

Deu.24.19#11.r: Someone living in Israel who was not born into it.
Deu.24.19#11.n: Gesenius: a person living out of his own country. STEPBible's lexicon: a newcomer lacking inherited rights. Inherited rights in Israel meant land, so the gēr would usually have no field of their own to reap. That last step is a reasonable reading, not something the lexicons state.

Deu.24.19#12.r: A child without a father to provide for them.
Deu.24.19#12.n: Gesenius notes the word is used of a child who has lost only its father. So 'fatherless', which every translation here uses, is more exact than 'orphan'.

Deu.24.19#13.r: A woman without a husband to provide for her.

Deu.24.19#14.r: The sheaf now belongs to these three.
Deu.24.19#14.n: The Hebrew says simply 'it shall be', and the 'to the' on each of the three nouns makes it ownership: it is theirs. The Douay-Rheims follows the Latin Vulgate here and rewords the clause entirely.
t: thou shalt suffer ... to take it away

Deu.24.19#15.r: Gives the purpose of the law.

Deu.24.19#16.r: God's blessing is tied to the sheaf left behind.
Deu.24.19#16.n: Gesenius puts 'to bend the knees, to kneel' first among this verb's senses, ahead of 'to bless'.

Deu.24.19#17.r: The personal name of Israel's God.
Deu.24.19#17.n: The translations show four traditions for the name. The KJV, Geneva and Douay-Rheims say 'the Lord', the BSB uses small capitals (LORD), the ASV and YLT say 'Jehovah', and the JPS writes 'HaShem' ('the Name').

Deu.24.19#18.n: The form is plural but the meaning is singular. In our parsed copy, Gesenius here is only a cross-reference to another entry.

Deu.24.19#19.r: No part of your work is left out of the blessing.

Deu.24.19#21.r: The hands that cut the sheaf.
Deu.24.19#21.n: The form is dual, 'your two hands'. Hebrew uses the dual for things that come in pairs.

Heb.7.8#01.r: Adds the next step of the argument.

Heb.7.8#02.r: In the one case: the Levitical priests.
Heb.7.8#02.n: The BSB writes 'In the case of the Levites', which names who 'here' means. That is a fair reading of the chapter, but the word itself is only 'here'.
t: In the case of the Levites

Heb.7.8#03.r: Sets up the contrast completed by 'but' in the second half.
Heb.7.8#03.n: Abbott-Smith calls this particle 'generally untranslatable'. It pairs with δέ later in the verse: here on the one hand, there on the other. Most translations leave it out.

Heb.7.8#04.r: The tenth part paid to the priests.
Heb.7.8#04.n: Abbott-Smith notes that the Septuagint uses this word for Hebrew מַעֲשֵׂר, the tithe, including at Genesis 14:20, where Abram gives the tenth to Melchizedek.

Heb.7.8#05.r: Men subject to death, set against the one who lives.
Heb.7.8#05.n: A present participle: literally 'dying men', men who are in the process of dying. The BSB's 'mortal' captures the contrast with 'he lives'.

Heb.7.8#07.r: The priests take in the tithe.
Heb.7.8#07.n: This is the same verb as 'having received' in Matthew 25:24 on this page. The BSB's 'collect' leans toward taxation language.

Heb.7.8#08.n: The Greek has no verb in this half. The KJV and Geneva supply 'he receiveth them', and the BSB names Melchizedek outright.

Heb.7.8#09.r: Completes the contrast opened by μέν.

Heb.7.8#10.n: The participle is passive: he is the one testified about. The writer does not say who testifies. The likeliest reading is the Scripture account of Melchizedek, but that is an inference.

Heb.7.8#11.r: Introduces the content of the testimony.

Heb.7.8#12.r: Present tense: he goes on living, set against the dying men.
Heb.7.8#12.n: The YLT's 'he was living' departs from the present tense of the Greek. The BSB's 'lives on' brings out the continuing sense.
